title: Corporate lobbying, political action committees, and market concentration
document_type: empirical academic journal article (open access, CC BY 4.0); accepted 11 September 2025
coverage: Full text read: 535cf83bf4d4.txt (73,035 chars) in five chunks, front matter through references and affiliations. Figures 1-4 are not in the text, so placebo and trend results are prose only. Paul markup: no _annots sidecar exists for this sha12 and annot_sha12s is empty, so paul_markup is empty and 0 items were dropped. Paul's 4 annotated-bibliography entries in paul_entries were used as context only. Metadata confirmed: title, DOI, year 2025, venue Public Choice; authors corrected from surnames to full names. Paul's entries state 7.5% to 10.5%; the paper says 7.4% to 10.5% (conclusion: 7% to 10.5%). Paul's 17 Oct 2025 date is not in the text (acceptance 11 Sept 2025). The paper has no limitations section.
research_question: Do firms' political activities (corporate lobbying and PAC contributions) raise their share of industry sales, assets or market capitalization, and is any such association causal rather than reflecting larger firms lobbying more?
theory: Public choice rent-seeking (Tullock 1967; Stigler 1971; Tollison 1982) and policymaker rent extraction (McChesney 1987, 1997; Coate and McChesney 1992). Political connections are argued to create barriers to entry and weaken competition, raising market concentration.
data: Compustat firm financials merged by company name with Center for Responsive Politics lobbying and PAC data (from Senate Office of Public Records disclosures). About 26,500 unique firms. Annual panel 1998-2016: 237,849 firm-year observations for the baseline ShareAssets regressions (116,242 with complete controls); text says roughly 250,000. Lobbying in 4.23 percent of firm-years; mean LobbyAmt 33,764 dollars, maximum above 45 million. PAC tests use election years: N = 62,198 (Table 6) and 62,558 (Table 7). Difference-in-differences uses quarterly data 2003Q1 to 2009Q1 with N = 139,711 in full-control specifications. Unit of observation is the firm within NAICS industry.
method: OLS panel regressions of firm market share (firm total divided by NAICS industry total for assets, market cap or sales) on a Lobby indicator or ln(LobAmt+1), with firm controls (Assets, D/E, current ratio, ROE, asset turnover, profit margin, price range, share turnover), industry and year fixed effects, and firm-clustered standard errors. PAC regressions use PAC, DemPAC and GopPAC indicators, then WinPAC, LosePAC and OtherPAC split by election outcome. Robustness: univariate correlations, industry-by-lobbying interactions, exclusion of top and bottom 5 percent by market cap, SIC instead of NAICS codes.
identification: Difference-in-differences around the Abramoff guilty plea (3 January 2006), with Post = 2006Q1 to 2009Q1. Treated firms are lobbying firms (Lobby or ln amount); controls are non-lobbying firms. Eq. 3 includes Treatment, Post, the interaction, controls, and industry and year fixed effects; no firm fixed effects are stated. Parallel pre-trends checked visually (Fig. 1). Five randomly drawn placebo event dates (Figs 2-4). Strategy follows Borisov, Goldman and Gupta (2016), who treat the plea as a negative shock to lobbying returns.
scope: Firms in Compustat matched to CRP lobbying and PAC data, 1998-2016 for annual tests and 2003-2009 for the event study. Post-1998 lobbying disclosure era. US firms implied by the Senate and Abramoff context. Concentration measured within NAICS industries. Not a full population of firms, since only name-matched firms enter.
measures: ShareAssets, ShareMcap, ShareSales (firm share of NAICS industry total assets, market cap or revenue); Lobby (positive lobbying expenditures in year); LobbyAmt and ln(LobAmt+1); PAC, DemPAC, GopPAC (party of recipients); WinPAC, LosePAC, OtherPAC (election outcome); Treatment x Post; controls listed under method.

key_findings.finding: Cross-section: lobbying firms have higher industry concentration. Lobby coefficient on ShareAssets is 0.0907 with no controls and 0.0743 with full controls, described as about 7.4 percent higher.
Same pattern for ShareMcap and ShareSales: Lobby coefficients 0.0996 and 0.0804 (market cap) and 0.0936 and 0.0759 (sales), baseline and full-controls.
key_findings.numbers: ShareSales text range 7.6 to 9.9 percent; ShareMcap text 'more than 8 percent'

key_findings.finding: Lobbying intensity: ln(LobAmt+1) is positive and significant across measures and specifications.
key_findings.numbers: ShareAssets 0.0078 baseline, 0.0062 with controls; SE 0.0007 and 0.0008

key_findings.finding: PAC contributors have about 11 percent higher concentration than non-contributors, with full controls and industry and year fixed effects.
Party split: DemPAC and GopPAC coefficients are similar and significant, so the authors find no systematic partisan difference.
Winning-candidate PAC money drives the PAC result; contributions to losing candidates show no effect.
key_findings.numbers: WinPAC 0.0620, 0.0710, 0.0603 (significant at 5 percent); LosePAC 0.0404, 0.0306, 0.0423 (not significant); OtherPAC 0.0495, 0.0696, 0.0504

key_findings.finding: Abramoff plea DiD, assets: Treatment x Post falls relative to non-lobbying firms, a 2.65 percent relative decline in the three post years with full controls; authors say over 30 percent of the pre-event average.
key_findings.location: Section 4.4, Table 9 column 3 and column 6 text

key_findings.finding: Abramoff plea DiD, market cap: larger decline in the full specification, read as a 3.4 percent relative drop.
key_findings.numbers: Lobby -0.0336 (SE 0.0099); ln -0.0030 (SE 0.0008); all significant at 1 percent

key_findings.finding: Abramoff plea DiD, sales: full specification significant at 5 percent; reduced specification not significant.
Placebo: the actual Abramoff estimate lies below the lower bound of the placebo confidence intervals for all three concentration measures, which the authors read as a causal response.
key_findings.location: Section 4.4, Figures 2-4 (prose only; no placebo table)
key_findings.numbers: Five random placebo dates plus their average; no numeric placebo values given in text

key_findings.finding: Pre-trend caveat: lobbying firms' concentration begins to fall in late 2004, before the January 2006 plea. The authors attribute this to the Senate Indian Affairs Committee investigation and still judge parallel trends satisfied.
key_findings.location: Section 4.4, text after Fig. 1 discussion; Fig. 1

key_findings.finding: Robustness claims not tabulated: industry-by-lobbying interactions leave results intact; excluding top and bottom 5 percent by market cap keeps Lobby, ln and PAC significant; SIC codes give similar results.

limitations: Paper has no limitations section; the caveats below are the ones the authors state or that the design text makes explicit.
Pre-event decline in lobbying firms' concentration starts late 2004, before the 3 January 2006 plea; authors attribute it to the investigation.
Causal claim rests on one event shock with three post years (2006Q1-2009Q1); placebo dates are randomly drawn and placebo values are shown only in figures.
Robustness checks (SIC codes, industry interactions, excluding top and bottom 5 percent) are described but not tabulated.
Lobbying and PAC data are matched to Compustat by company name; match quality is not evaluated in the text.
Stated specifications include industry and year fixed effects but no firm fixed effects.

Internal inconsistencies: text says roughly 250,000 observations versus 237,849 in tables; Table 6 and 7 notes say 1998-2018 while text says 2000-2016 election years; Table 8 caption describes 2003Q1-2005Q4 while text describes 2003Q1-2009Q1; intro gives 1.8 to 3.4 percent versus Table 9 to 10 coefficients of -2.65 and -3.36 percent.
Lobbying is rare (4.23 percent of firm-years) and heavily skewed; the authors report intensity results alongside the indicator.

short_quotes.quote: lobbying firms experienced a significant decline in market concentration, relative to non-lobbying firms
